patch.value: Retention and lawful erasure over an immutable history: a decades-long record needs a policy that deletes without breaking proof

The project's durability promise is that every mutation is permanently recorded and any item is restorable to any version. Over a multi-decade horizon that promise collides with three obligations no current item owns: statutory erasure requests against personal data that entered an item body or a history patch, contractual retention limits that require records to be destroyed on a schedule, and storage economics for streams that only ever grow. The mechanisms partly exist and are unreconciled. history-redact rewrites literals and recomputes hashes, history-compact replaces a prefix with a synthetic baseline, and history-repair re-anchors a drifted chain — but there is no policy layer deciding when any of them must run, no statement of what a redaction is permitted to destroy versus obliged to preserve, and no proof that a stream which has been redacted and then compacted is still independently verifiable a decade later by a reader who has none of the intervening tooling. The open format specification will make the bytes readable in twenty years; nothing yet makes them lawfully retainable for twenty years.

The workspace can declare retention classes and schedules as configuration, and the classification of an item or field is data rather than convention; An erasure request resolves to a deterministic set of streams, entries and fields, and the operation reports exactly what it destroyed and what it preserved; A stream that has been redacted and then compacted still verifies end to end for a reader holding only the format specification and the published verification rule; The policy distinguishes what may be destroyed from what must survive — the fact that a mutation occurred, its ordering, its author class, and the chain linkage — so proof of process survives destruction of content; Destructive policy operations are themselves recorded as audited events that cannot be removed by a later run of the same policy; A tombstone is left wherever content was removed so a later reader sees a deliberate absence and not silent corruption; Small workspaces with no declared policy behave exactly as today with no new required configuration
Reconcile immutable proof with the obligation to delete, so neither promise is quietly abandoned
The tracker remains adoptable by organisations with statutory retention and erasure duties instead of being disqualified by its own durability guarantee
Determines whether pm can hold decades of institutional context in regulated settings or only in ones with no deletion obligations
A declared retention and erasure policy model, enforced by the existing history maintenance primitives, with verifiability preserved across every permitted destructive operation
Redaction, compaction and repair have all shipped independently; the policy that should govern them is the missing layer, and retrofitting it after adoption is far harder
